abstract: Cell membranes are decorated by dense, polymeric macromolecules such as proteins with bulky intrinsically disordered regions, glycosylated proteins, and glycopolymers. Experiments have illustrated that the curvature of cellular membranes, which plays a role in diverse biological processes, can be regulated by the local density of these membrane-tethered polymers and their response to environmental changes. However, the mechanisms underlying the feedback between solution conditions, membrane curvature, and the local density and molecular weight of membrane-tethered polymers remain largely unexplored. In this work, using a combination of theory and experiment, we show that the ionic strength of the surrounding solution and the degree of ionization both play important roles in regulating the conformation of the membrane-tethered polymers, which in turn influences their membrane curvature generation capabilities. Specifically, we show that for negatively charged, disordered proteins and glycans, the thickness of the polymer brush decreases with ionic strength but increases with grafting density and degree of ionization, resulting in enhanced sensitivity to membrane curvature and an amplified ability to drive membrane curvature at lower ionic concentrations. Our findings reveal a mechanism by which membrane-tethered polymers generate membrane curvature to minimize free energy, with the extent of curvature generation modulated by the polymer grafting density and layer thickness, as well as by the ionic strength of the surrounding solution. The implications of these findings are broad, suggesting that perturbations to biopolymer charge, such as sialylation of glycans and phosphorylation of disordered proteins, could actively modulate membrane curvature induction in diverse cellular processes from endocytosis to cell motility.
